title: Dropping the Needle
statement: A floor has parallel lines spaced $1$ unit apart. A needle of length $1$ is dropped at a random position and angle. What is the probability that it crosses a line? Try to answer without integrating over the angle.
insight: The expected number of crossings is linear in length for any rigid curve (Buffon's noodle). A circle of diameter 1 always crosses exactly twice and has length π, so a length-1 needle crosses 2/π times on average.
redHerring: Computing the double integral over center position and angle (correct, but it misses the elegant argument).
hints: For a needle of length 1, crossing at most once, $P(\text{cross}) = E[\#\text{crossings}]$.
Split a long needle into pieces: expected crossings add up. So $E[\#\text{crossings}] = c\cdot\text{length}$ for straight needles, and in fact for any bent wire.
Find a shape whose number of crossings you know for sure, wherever it lands.
solution:
Since a length-1 needle crosses at most once, $P(\text{cross}) = E[X]$ where $X$ counts crossings.

By linearity, cutting any rigid wire into small pieces shows $E[X] = c\cdot L$ for a wire of length $L$, whatever its shape. A circle of diameter $1$ (length $\pi$) always crosses the lines exactly twice, so $c\pi = 2$ and $c = \tfrac2\pi$.

So $P(\text{cross}) = \tfrac2\pi \approx 0.6366$.
